newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish scientists find possible new human species.
newsitem.headline: Spanish scientists find possible new human species.

text.p: A group of Spanish scientists said on Thursday they had discovered a new species of human beings in a 780,000-year-old fossil, possibly the oldest known European.
"We believe this is a new species that we have called Homo antecessor," Jose Maria Bermudez de Castro of the National Museum of Natural Sciences in Madrid told a news conference.
"It's a species that we consider the common ancestor of modern humanity and the Neanderthals."

Bermudez de Castro and a team of Spanish paleoanthropologists found the fossilised remains of a boy with a remarkably modern face in a limestone cave in Spain's central Atapuerca mountains during an excavation from 1994 to 1996.

They said the unique combination of features, with a face like the modern Homo sapiens species and a jaw and brow similar to the extinct Neanderthals, led them to name a new species, a finding to be published in the U.S. journal Science on Friday.
The boy was discovered among a group of six people of almost modern height and bone size with a relatively advanced cognitive ability, as judged by the quality of tools found near them.
"This is clearly a very important new finding," Richard Gallagher, European editor of the journal Science, told reporters.
"These are bold, exciting proposals that already have the field buzzing."

The Spanish team acknowledged that the decision to name a new species based on the reconstructed remains of just one boy -- the faces of the adults in the cave were not as markedly modern -- was controversial.
"We think we have enough information to define it in the proper sense of a new species," said Antonio Rosas, another paleoanthropologist at the National Museum of Natural Sciences.
"But people are probably going to need some time to accommodate this proposal."

The find, with more than 80 fossils of skulls, jaws, teeth and other parts of the skeleton, will offer new insight into a mysterious time and place in human evolution, according to a research news article to be published in Science.
"We now have a better window on the first people of the European continent," paleoanthropologist Philip Rightmire of the State University of New York at Binghamton told the journal.

The Atapuerca fossils are particularly valuable because they are well-dated, using shifts in the Earth's magnetic field, to about 800,000 years ago. They help fill a big gap in the fossil record of tracing the evolutionary path to modern man.
There are various, competing theories on when human beings first arrived in Europe.

But if the Spanish scientists are correct, it would appear that the H. antecessor, a name that comes from the Latin word for explorer, originated in Africa where it gave rise to the H. sapiens long before that species migrated to Europe.

According to the new theory, the H. antecessor also trekked into Europe about a million years ago and gave rise to the Homo heidelbergensis, the predecessor of the Neandertal man who lived in ice age Europe until about 28,000 years ago.
Therefore the H. antecessor, and not the H. heidelbergensis as previously believed, is the true common ancestor of both the Neanderthals and modern human beings.
But the theory, which uses a few dental and cranial features to link H. antecessor with 1.6 million-year-old fossils from East Africa, is seen as a big leap.

"I think many of my colleagues will be uncomfortable with creating a new species, because it is mainly based on the facial features of one juvenile," paleoanthropologist Jean-Jacques Hubil of the National Centre for Scientific Research in Paris, France, told Science.
The Spanish team is excited about the theory because it fits other views about fossils found in Africa, Asia and Europe.
"For the moment these are simply guesses...We are hoping that new discoveries will confirm our hypothesis," said Juan Luis Arsuaga, another co-leader of the Spanish scientific team.
"But in any case, this was not a capricious theory. We tried in every way to compare these remains with any other species that was already known."
